body:
OPERATOR PROPOSAL, filed as STORY-1414, draft/High. It is the structural fix for the failure that has cost us two rebuild scrambles today, and the mechanism is already written — pointed at a different process.

THEIR IDEA, in their words: a flag so a spawned implementer uses only the aida corresponding to the latest hash on main, requesting a build for that hash and re-execing into it when available.

THE PRIOR ART THAT MAKES THIS CHEAP. `aida-cli-lib/src/mcp.rs` already does exactly this for the MCP server:

    198  fn check() -> Option<McpRespawnPlan>            query the on-disk binary identity
    201  mcp_binary_is_newer_or_different(running, on_disk)
    213  fn respawn(plan)      "detected newer binary on disk; self-respawning"
    292  fn exec_mcp_respawn(plan)                       command.exec()

A long-running MCP server notices a newer binary and re-execs into it. The drain — where staleness does the most damage — has none of this, despite already recording `binary_sha` in drain.lock at wave start. It knows what it is pinned to; nothing compares that to HEAD.

WHERE I PUT THE GATE, and why not where the operator first suggested. They said "if you spawn an implementer". I moved it to WAVE LAUNCH rather than per-implementer, because a wave pins one binary for all members and swapping mid-wave is what `AFTER_WAVE=1` already refuses — correctly, since members would otherwise run under different orchestration semantics inside one batch. Per-implementer freshness reintroduces exactly that hazard. Launch is the only boundary where re-exec is both safe and sufficient. Worth confirming you agree, because it is a change from what they described.

THE OPEN QUESTION I DELIBERATELY DID NOT ANSWER: what happens when the build fails. Refusing to launch halts every drain on a compile error — safe, total, and it converts a build break into a work stoppage. Launching stale with a loud record keeps work moving on known-old orchestration. I lean refuse, and I wrote that lean into the spec as a lean rather than a decision, because the cost is real and disposition is yours.

WHY THIS IS WORTH A HIGH RATHER THAN A PAPERCUT. Today's two instances were not close calls. The first ran four orchestrator fixes' worth of stale code for five and a half hours and nearly had me requeue eight specs into a guard that was not running. The second had your reviewer writing unstamped verdicts for three hours after the fix that stamps them had merged — and the reviewer caught it, not the system. Both times the only signal was `aida pull`'s "your aida binary is now behind HEAD", which was ignored twice, once by me after I had written myself a rule about exactly this.

A warning that is ignored twice in one day by the people who wrote the rule is not a control.
